title: Sperm health & DNA fragmentation
summary: Sperm are unusually exposed to oxidative damage: their membranes are packed with oxidisable fatty acids, they have almost no cytoplasm for antioxidant enzymes, and they cannot repair oxidised DNA themselves, so the egg has to. High sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF) is linked to slower natural conception, roughly double the miscarriage risk and lower IVF/ICSI success. The biggest proven levers are treating a clinical varicocele, stopping smoking, avoiding testicular heat and exogenous testosterone, and ejaculating every 1-2 days; diet, weight and exercise help modestly. Over-the-counter 'male fertility' antioxidants have mostly failed in large, well-run trials (MOXI, FAZST), so they are a low priority, and megadoses may do harm.

factors.name: Clinical varicocele (enlarged scrotal veins)
factors.headline: A palpable varicocele is the single largest common driver of high SDF, adding roughly 10-14 percentage points on average.

dose.effective: Clinical (palpable, grade 1-3) varicocele found on physical exam; ultrasound-only (subclinical) varicoceles matter much less.
dose.studied_range: Present in roughly 40% of infertile men; meta-analyses compare men with vs without varicocele.
dose.too_much: Higher grades and bilateral varicoceles tend to do more damage, but the grade-SDF relationship is inconsistent.
dose.timeframe: Damage accumulates over years; after repair SDF falls over 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Ask a urologist for a scrotal exam if SDF is high, semen is abnormal or there is a dull ache or visible veins.

factors.mechanism: Venous pooling raises testicular temperature and causes hypoxia and reflux of adrenal/renal metabolites; this drives mitochondrial ROS, NADPH oxidase activity in leukocytes and lipid peroxidation, producing 8-OHdG and strand breaks in poorly protaminated sperm.
factors.interactions: Heat from [sauna-hot-baths] and [everyday-scrotal-heat] adds to the varicocele's thermal load. Smoking [smoking-sperm] in varicocele patients compounds oxidative stress. The fix is [varicocele-repair], not supplements.
factors.caveats: Many men with varicocele are fertile; it is a problem mainly when semen or SDF is abnormal. Varicocele and SDF studies are mostly cross-sectional.

factors.name: Varicocele repair (microsurgical varicocelectomy or embolisation)
factors.headline: Repairing a clinical varicocele lowers SDF by about 7 percentage points on average, and more when SDF starts high.

dose.effective: One procedure (microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy is the reference technique) in men with a palpable varicocele plus abnormal semen or high SDF.
dose.studied_range: 19 studies, 1070 men; SCSA, TUNEL and SCD all showed reductions.
dose.timeframe: Re-test semen/SDF about 3-6 months after surgery; one spermatogenic cycle is ~64-74 days.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: consider varicocelectomy in men trying to conceive with palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen (not azoospermia). EAU adds that the female partner should have good ovarian reserve, because the benefit takes months.

factors.mechanism: Removes venous reflux, restoring testicular cooling and oxygenation and cutting seminal ROS, which lowers oxidative DNA damage in newly made sperm.
factors.interactions: Lifestyle changes ([smoking-sperm], [sauna-hot-baths]) should be made in parallel. If the female partner is older, time may favour going straight to ART, optionally with [testicular-sperm-icsi] or short abstinence [short-abstinence].
factors.caveats: The SDF drop is solid; the pregnancy benefit is less certain (Cochrane: pregnancy RR 1.55, low certainty; live birth uncertain). Not useful for subclinical varicocele with normal semen.

factors.name: Exogenous testosterone (TRT) and anabolic-androgenic steroids
factors.headline: Outside testosterone shuts down the brain's signal (LH/FSH) to the testes and can drop sperm counts to zero; recovery takes months to over a year.

dose.effective: Any exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid, including gels, injections and 'cycles'.
dose.studied_range: Androgen regimens used for male contraception reliably suppress sperm output.
dose.too_much: Long-term, high-dose and long-acting preparations recover slowest.
dose.timeframe: Median recovery to 20 million/mL about 3.4 months after contraceptive-style androgen use; after steroid abuse, often 6-12+ months, sometimes incomplete.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: do not prescribe testosterone to men who want current or future fertility. Do not stop abruptly without medical advice; urologists can use hCG, SERMs or aromatase inhibitors to restart production.

factors.mechanism: Negative feedback suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH; intratesticular testosterone collapses, halting spermatogenesis (endocrine, not primarily oxidative).
factors.interactions: Overrides any benefit from diet or supplements. Often combined with other harmful exposures in body-building (high-dose supplements, stimulants).
factors.caveats: Not an SDF factor in the usual sense: it mainly lowers sperm number, often to azoospermia. Included because it is the most common avoidable cause of severe male-factor infertility in young men.

factors.name: Genital tract infection and leukocytospermia
factors.headline: Active infection (e.g. Chlamydia, Mycoplasma) and white cells in semen raise ROS and SDF; treating a proven infection can lower SDF by about a third.

dose.effective: Leukocytospermia is defined as >=1 million white cells/mL; even 0.2-1 million/mL has been linked to higher ROS and SDF.
dose.studied_range: Antibiotic courses guided by culture/PCR; follow-up about 4 months.
dose.timeframe: In one study SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2% after ~3.8 months of treatment; pregnancy rates were higher in couples who tried after rather than during treatment.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: if round cells exceed 1 million/mL, distinguish white cells from immature germ cells before treating. Treat confirmed infection; do not give empiric antibiotics for every abnormal semen test.

factors.mechanism: Activated neutrophils and macrophages produce superoxide via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) at rates far above sperm, overwhelming seminal antioxidants and attacking sperm membranes and DNA.
factors.interactions: [febrile-illness] from the same infection adds thermal damage. Antioxidants are not a substitute for treating infection.
factors.caveats: A large meta-analysis found overall effects of Chlamydia and HPV on SDF negligible, so the strongest data are from symptomatic or culture-positive cases. Evidence comes from small observational studies.

factors.name: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)
factors.headline: A fever of 39-40 C for even 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.

dose.effective: Body temperature around 38.5-40 C for 1 day or more.
dose.studied_range: Case report: 2 days at 39-40 C followed for 79 days.
dose.timeframe: DFI up 24-36% at days 15-37, back toward baseline by about day 79; plan semen tests or ART cycles at least ~3 months after a high fever if possible.
dose.notes: Fever control with paracetamol/acetaminophen is reasonable; there is no evidence that it prevents the sperm effect.

factors.mechanism: Whole-body hyperthermia warms the testes, impairing late spermatogenesis and chromatin protamination and increasing heat-shock and apoptotic signalling.
factors.interactions: Same mechanism as [sauna-hot-baths]. A semen test taken within 3 months of a fever may overstate long-term problems.
factors.caveats: Evidence is mostly case reports and small series; the effect is temporary.

factors.name: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high
factors.headline: Sperm taken directly from the testis have about 25 percentage points less DNA fragmentation than ejaculated sperm, and pooled studies show higher pregnancy and live birth with ICSI.

dose.effective: Testicular sperm aspiration/extraction (TESA/TESE) for ICSI in non-azoospermic men with confirmed high SDF, usually after failed IVF/ICSI or recurrent miscarriage.
dose.studied_range: 5 studies with paired SDF (143 men); 4 studies, 507 cycles with clinical outcomes.
dose.too_much: Invasive; small risks of bleeding, infection and testicular damage; testicular sperm have higher aneuploidy in some studies.
dose.timeframe: Single procedure at the time of egg retrieval.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM 2024: may consider. EAU: experimental (weak). Try reversible causes and short-abstinence ejaculates first; a meta-analysis found testicular SDF ~9.5 points lower than short-abstinence ejaculates.

factors.mechanism: Much oxidative DNA damage occurs during epididymal transit and storage, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS; testicular sperm bypass this exposure.
factors.interactions: Compare with [short-abstinence], which reduces epididymal storage time non-invasively.
factors.caveats: Evidence is from small, mostly non-randomised studies. Not appropriate as first-line care.

factors.name: Tobacco smoking
factors.headline: Smokers average about 9 percentage points higher SDF and lower count, motility and morphology; quitting improves semen within 3-6 months.

dose.effective: Quit completely; harm rises with cigarettes per day (moderate/heavy smokers, roughly >10/day, show larger effects).
dose.studied_range: Light (<10/day) to heavy (>20/day) smokers in clinic and population samples.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified; avoid second-hand smoke too.
dose.timeframe: Semen improved at 3 months and further at 6 months after quitting.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement is far less harmful than smoking. Vaping data for sperm are sparse.

factors.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers oxidants, cadmium, lead and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; seminal leukocytes and ROS rise, antioxidant levels fall, and sperm show more 8-OHdG and strand breaks.
factors.interactions: Stacks with [varicocele] and [air-pollution-sperm]. Non-responders to stopping heat exposure in one series were mostly smokers. Antioxidant pills do not offset smoking.
factors.caveats: Effects on standard semen parameters are moderate; the clearest harm is on DNA integrity and on offspring and partner health.

factors.name: Saunas, hot tubs and hot baths
factors.headline: Regular sauna or hot-tub use reversibly damages sperm count, motility and chromatin packaging; effects take 3-6 months to clear.

dose.effective: Avoid while trying to conceive. Harm shown with sauna at 80-90 C for 15 min twice a week for 3 months, and with scrotal water at 43 C for 30 min on 10 occasions.
dose.studied_range: Sauna 80-90 C x 15 min, 2x/week, 12 weeks; scrotal bath 43 C x 30 min, daily or every 3 days, 10 sessions; habitual hot tubs/baths.
dose.too_much: Testes work best about 2-4 C below core temperature; any wet heat above ~40 C held for 30 min is a risk. Daily (consecutive) exposure was worse than intermittent.
dose.timeframe: Recovery by about 16 weeks after short exposure and fully by 6 months after 3 months of sauna use.
dose.notes: If you will not give it up, keep sessions short, sit with the scrotum away from hot surfaces, and stop for at least 3 months before trying.

factors.mechanism: Scrotal hyperthermia disrupts histone-to-protamine exchange and mitochondrial function in developing sperm, raises heat-shock and hypoxia gene expression and triggers apoptosis, making DNA more susceptible to oxidative breaks.
factors.interactions: Adds to [varicocele] and [everyday-scrotal-heat]. Same pathway as [febrile-illness].
factors.caveats: Trials are small (10-20 normozoospermic men), but they are interventional with clear reversal, so causality is convincing. Benefits of sauna for cardiovascular health are real; this is a temporary trade-off.

factors.name: Laptops on the lap, tight underwear, long sitting, occupational heat
factors.headline: Everyday heat sources raise scrotal temperature 1-3 C; boxer wearers have about 25% higher sperm concentration, but direct SDF data are thin.

dose.effective: Laptop on a desk, not the lap; looser underwear (boxers); stand or walk for a few minutes every 30-60 min; heat protection or breaks for hot jobs (bakers, welders, drivers).
dose.studied_range: Laptop sessions of 60 min; scrotal temperature +1 C within 11-28 min.
dose.too_much: A laptop on closed thighs raised scrotal temperature 2.6-2.8 C in 60 min; lap pads did not prevent it.
dose.timeframe: Benefits, if any, would appear after one spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Sitting with legs apart reduces the rise. Heated car seats are plausible but unstudied for sperm.

factors.mechanism: Mild, repeated scrotal hyperthermia: same thermal pathway as saunas but smaller in size.
factors.interactions: Additive with [sauna-hot-baths] and [varicocele].
factors.caveats: Underwear and laptop data are cross-sectional or physiological (temperature) studies; the underwear association was partly explained by FSH. Occupational heat is a recognised risk but studies are older and confounded.

factors.name: Obesity and metabolic dysfunction
factors.headline: Obese men are more often infertile and have lower IVF live-birth rates; the BMI-SDF link is real but smaller and less consistent than for smoking or varicocele.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30, ideally 18.5-25; waist reduction matters more than the scale number.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories from <18.5 to >=40.
dose.too_much: Risk rises steeply above BMI 35-40 (odds of oligo/azoospermia 2.04 in morbid obesity). Impaired glucose tolerance was linked to +13.8 points SDF.
dose.timeframe: Lifestyle weight loss over 3-6 months has improved semen in trials.
dose.notes: Very underweight (BMI <18.5) also trends toward worse semen.

factors.mechanism: Excess adipose tissue raises aromatase activity (lower testosterone, higher estradiol), systemic inflammation and insulin resistance, increases scrotal fat and temperature, and raises seminal ROS.
factors.interactions: Improves with [weight-loss-sperm], [exercise-moderate-sperm] and [mediterranean-diet-sperm]. Often co-occurs with poor sleep and sugary drinks.
factors.caveats: In the SDF meta-analysis only class I obesity showed a small, borderline increase (SMD 0.23). Confounding by diet, activity and diabetes is substantial.

factors.name: Weight loss through diet and exercise (in men with obesity)
factors.headline: Weight loss in obese men raises sperm concentration and motility and lowers DNA fragmentation (effect size about -0.7); lifestyle programmes beat bariatric surgery for semen.

dose.effective: Lose 5-15% of body weight over 3-6 months through diet plus exercise.
dose.studied_range: 12 studies, mean baseline BMI 45; residential programme with 15% median weight loss over 14 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid loss after bariatric surgery produced no clinically significant semen or DNA-damage improvement and may temporarily worsen semen; time conception carefully after surgery.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months; re-test semen after one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: GLP-1 drugs and metformin: too little sperm data to judge.

factors.mechanism: Reverses aromatase-driven hypogonadism, lowers inflammation and insulin resistance, and reduces scrotal heat, lowering seminal oxidative stress.
factors.interactions: Usually achieved via [mediterranean-diet-sperm] and [exercise-moderate-sperm]; those may help independently of the weight lost.
factors.caveats: Mostly uncontrolled before-after studies in severely obese men; little live-birth data.

factors.name: Paternal age
factors.headline: SDF rises steadily with age, with a clear jump after 50 (about +12.6 points on average), alongside more new mutations in offspring.

dose.effective: Not modifiable, but relevant to timing: SDF climbs from the 20s with no threshold; effects are largest from about age 45-50.
dose.studied_range: Men aged 20-80.
dose.too_much: Age >=50 associated with the largest SDF increase.
dose.timeframe: Lifelong, gradual.
dose.notes: Older men gain the most from removing other risk factors, because damage is additive. Partner's age matters too: older eggs repair paternal DNA damage less well.

factors.mechanism: Age-related decline in testicular antioxidant defence and mitochondrial function, more oxidative stress, less efficient apoptotic culling of damaged germ cells, and accumulating replication errors in spermatogonial stem cells.
factors.interactions: Combined with older maternal age, high SDF has a bigger effect on embryo quality and miscarriage (see [testicular-sperm-icsi]).
factors.caveats: Age is confounded with weight, illness and varicocele duration; the absolute risk to any one child remains low.

factors.name: Alcohol
factors.headline: Daily or heavy drinking lowers semen quality (about 33% lower concentration above 40 units/week); occasional light drinking shows little effect.

dose.effective: Keep intake at or below about 5 units (UK units, ~8 g alcohol each) per week while trying to conceive; avoid daily drinking.
dose.studied_range: From 0 to over 40 units/week in 1221 young Danish men; 15 cross-sectional studies (16,395 men).
dose.too_much: Adverse associations appear above ~5 units/week and are strongest above 25 units/week.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Binge drinking was not independently linked to semen in the Danish study, but heavy episodes are best avoided.

factors.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), lowers testosterone, raises estrogen and depletes antioxidants such as glutathione.
factors.interactions: Often clustered with [smoking-sperm] and [obesity-sperm].
factors.caveats: Direct SDF data are scarce; most evidence is on conventional parameters and is cross-sectional.

factors.name: Cannabis
factors.headline: Regular cannabis use is associated with more sperm DNA fragmentation and chromosome abnormalities in small studies.

dose.effective: Stop regular use at least 3 months before trying.
dose.studied_range: Regular users vs non-users in 54 infertile men.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Smoking cannabis also delivers combustion oxidants similar to tobacco.

factors.mechanism: THC acts on endocannabinoid receptors in the testis and sperm, disturbing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, spermatogenesis and mitochondrial function.
factors.interactions: Often co-used with tobacco [smoking-sperm].
factors.caveats: Exploratory, small, retrospective data; confounding by tobacco is likely.

factors.name: Air pollution
factors.headline: Periods of high air pollution are linked to higher SDF (about +9.7 points across studies) even when other semen measures look normal.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure on high-pollution days (air-quality alerts): avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors, keep car windows closed in traffic.
dose.studied_range: Episodes at or above US air-quality standard limits (Teplice, Czech Republic); PM and NO2 in later studies.
dose.timeframe: Effects appear in sperm produced during and after exposure (~2-3 months later).
dose.notes: Individual control is limited; the effect size is a population average.

factors.mechanism: Fine particles and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons cause systemic oxidative stress and inflammation, and some PAH metabolites form DNA adducts in germ cells.
factors.interactions: Additive with [smoking-sperm], which delivers similar compounds at much higher doses.
factors.caveats: Ecological and repeated-measures studies; exposure misclassification likely.

factors.name: Endocrine disruptors: phthalates and bisphenol A
factors.headline: Higher urinary phthalate and BPA levels are linked to more sperm DNA damage (about 10-18% more Comet damage per interquartile rise).

dose.effective: Practical reduction: avoid heating food in plastic, prefer glass/steel containers, eat less ultra-processed and canned food, choose fragrance-free personal care products.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary levels (median BPA 1.3 ng/mL).
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels fall within days; any sperm effect would take ~3 months.
dose.notes: No intervention trial shows that lowering exposure improves SDF.

factors.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and estrogenic receptor effects plus induction of oxidative stress in germ cells.
factors.interactions: Exposure falls naturally with a less processed diet ([mediterranean-diet-sperm]).
factors.caveats: Single-centre cross-sectional studies with spot urine samples; inconsistent replication.

factors.name: Pesticides (occupational and dietary)
factors.headline: Farm workers exposed to organophosphate/carbamate pesticides have higher SDF; high-residue produce seems to cancel the benefit of fruit and vegetables.

dose.effective: Use protective equipment for occupational spraying; wash produce; choose lower-residue or organic options for high-residue items if affordable.
dose.studied_range: Occupational cholinesterase-inhibiting exposure; dietary residues by produce type.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Do not cut fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides; the net effect of produce is positive or neutral.

factors.mechanism: Organophosphates generate ROS and lipid peroxidation in testis and disrupt the HPG axis.
factors.interactions: See [fruit-vegetables-sperm].
factors.caveats: Small cross-sectional occupational studies; dietary findings come from one cohort.

factors.name: Short or poor-quality sleep
factors.headline: Sleeping under 6 hours or over 9 hours, or poor sleep quality, is associated with roughly 15-20% lower sperm counts, but estimates are imprecise.

dose.effective: 7-9 hours per night with regular timing.
dose.studied_range: <6 h, 7-8.9 h and >=9 h per night; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index >5 vs <=5.
dose.too_much: Both short and long sleep were associated with lower counts.
dose.timeframe: Unknown; plausibly one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: No SDF-specific human data.

factors.mechanism: Sleep loss lowers testosterone and raises systemic inflammation and oxidative stress.
factors.interactions: Interlinked with [obesity-sperm].
factors.caveats: Observational; confidence intervals mostly cross zero.

factors.name: Mobile phone radiofrequency exposure
factors.headline: Lab studies show phone radiation can raise ROS in semen in a dish, but human studies are inconsistent and show no dose-response with hours of use.

dose.effective: Low-cost precaution: keep the phone out of the front trouser pocket when possible.
dose.studied_range: In vitro exposure of semen samples; self-reported daily use in observational studies.
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Treat as a weak, uncertain factor; far below smoking, heat or varicocele.

factors.mechanism: Proposed: RF energy and local heating increase mitochondrial ROS in sperm (shown in vitro), without clear DNA damage in the key in vitro study.
factors.interactions: Far smaller and less certain than heat sources in [everyday-scrotal-heat].
factors.caveats: One meta-analysis found no effect in human studies; another found associations but no dose-response, which argues against a strong causal effect. Confounding (sedentary habits, socioeconomic factors) likely.

factors.name: High-volume cycling
factors.headline: Cycling 5 or more hours a week is linked to lower sperm concentration; moderate cycling is not a concern.

dose.effective: Under about 5 hours/week is fine; above that, use a well-fitted saddle, padded shorts and rest days.
dose.studied_range: Cycling >=5 h/week vs no regular exercise (2261 men); 16 weeks of intensive road training (24 cyclists).
dose.too_much: Intensive training raised seminal inflammatory cytokines, with some semen changes persisting 30 days after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Recovery may need more than 30 days; plan ~3 months.
dose.notes: Combine with general exercise advice ([exercise-moderate-sperm]).

factors.mechanism: Perineal pressure, scrotal heat and friction, plus inflammation and oxidative stress from very high training loads.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [everyday-scrotal-heat].
factors.caveats: Observational; the training study comes from a group with several retracted papers.

key_numbers.label: Odds of low concentration, cycling >=5 h/week

factors.name: Frequent ejaculation (short abstinence, 1-2 days)
factors.headline: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps sperm fresher: each extra day of abstinence adds about 0.65 points of SDF, and a second sample 3 hours after the first cut SDF from 35% to 24%.

dose.effective: Ejaculate (intercourse or otherwise) every 1-2 days through the fertile window and beyond. For ART with high SDF, ask about a sample after 1 day or a second sample 1-4 hours after a first ejaculation.
dose.studied_range: Abstinence from 1-4 hours to 7+ days; 2-day cut-off in RCT meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Volume and total count fall with very frequent ejaculation, but for natural conception daily intercourse is not harmful.
dose.timeframe: Immediate: works on the next ejaculate.
dose.notes: Diagnostic labs usually specify 2-7 days of abstinence and SDF guidelines suggest 2-5 days before a test; follow the lab's instructions when testing, and use short abstinence for conception attempts and ART samples.

factors.mechanism: Shortens the time sperm sit in the epididymis, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS and stored sperm accumulate oxidative DNA damage.
factors.interactions: Cheapest and fastest lever; a non-invasive alternative to [testicular-sperm-icsi]. Works alongside slower changes that act on sperm production.
factors.caveats: One large meta-analysis of risk factors found no significant abstinence effect, and absolute reductions in healthy men are small (about 2-3 points). The biggest drops are in men with high baseline SDF or abnormal semen.

factors.name: Moderate regular exercise (and less sitting)
factors.headline: Active men have better sperm counts, and one large RCT found moderate continuous training improved sperm DNA integrity more than high-intensity training.

dose.effective: About 30-45 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise (brisk walking, jogging, swimming, gym cardio), 3-5 days a week, plus less TV/sitting time.
dose.studied_range: Moderate continuous, high-intensity continuous and interval training, 3 sessions/week for 24 weeks (280 men); >=15 h/week moderate-vigorous activity in observational data.
dose.too_much: Very high training loads and long-distance cycling may worsen semen ([cycling-sperm]); in the RCT moderate beat high-intensity.
dose.timeframe: Improvements by 12-24 weeks; benefits faded within about a month of stopping training.
dose.notes: Over 20 h/week of TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

factors.mechanism: Regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase) via hormetic Nrf2 signalling, lowers inflammation, improves insulin sensitivity and weight.
factors.interactions: Supports [weight-loss-sperm]. High-dose antioxidant pills can blunt exercise adaptations in other tissues, a reason not to stack them.
factors.caveats: The key RCTs come from one Iranian group (Hajizadeh Maleki/Tartibian); its moderate-exercise trial in infertile men (Cytokine 2017) and its combined-exercise trial (J Strength Cond Res 2019) were retracted, so the remaining healthy-men trial should be treated with caution. Observational data are confounded.

factors.name: Mediterranean / 'prudent' dietary pattern
factors.headline: Men who eat a Mediterranean or 'prudent' diet have better counts and motility (about +24 million sperm, +8.8 points motility), but fertility outcomes are untested.

dose.effective: Daily: vegetables (3+ servings), fruit (2+), whole grains, legumes several times a week, nuts (30-60 g), olive oil as main fat; fish 2+ times a week; little processed meat, sweets or sugary drinks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore tertiles; observational studies in 2558 men plus 2 small RCTs.
dose.timeframe: About 3 months for sperm-level effects.
dose.notes: The pattern matters more than any single 'superfood'.

factors.mechanism: Supplies dietary antioxidants (vitamin E, carotenoids, polyphenols), omega-3 fats, folate and zinc at food-level doses; lowers inflammation and insulin resistance.
factors.interactions: Contains [nuts-walnuts-sperm], [fish-omega3-sperm], [fruit-vegetables-sperm] and [tomatoes-lycopene-sperm]; displaces [processed-meat-sperm] and [sugary-drinks-sperm].
factors.caveats: Almost all data are cross-sectional or cohort studies; SDF itself is rarely measured; high heterogeneity (I2 ~80-90%).

factors.name: Walnuts and mixed nuts
factors.headline: Two RCTs found that adding 60-75 g of nuts a day improved sperm vitality, motility and morphology, and one also lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: 60 g/day mixed nuts (walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts) or 75 g/day walnuts (about a large handful to two handfuls), added to the usual diet.
dose.studied_range: 60 g/day for 14 weeks (FERTINUTS, n=119); 75 g/day walnuts for 12 weeks (n=117).
dose.too_much: 75 g walnuts is about 490 kcal; swap for other snacks to avoid weight gain. Avoid if allergic.
dose.timeframe: 12-14 weeks.
dose.notes: Unsalted, unroasted or dry-roasted nuts were used. Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3).

factors.mechanism: Provides ALA omega-3, vitamin E, polyphenols, magnesium, selenium and zinc; raised blood omega-3 and correlated with lower sperm aneuploidy; FERTINUTS showed lower SDF and miR-34b-3p expression.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet-sperm] and [fish-omega3-sperm].
factors.caveats: Healthy young men on Western diets; not infertile men; no pregnancy outcomes; FERTINUTS was partly funded by the nut industry.

factors.name: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)
factors.headline: Fish eaters have higher sperm counts, and a small RCT of 1.5 g/day DHA lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel, herring) 2-3 times a week; if supplementing, about 1-1.5 g/day EPA+DHA.
dose.studied_range: 1.5 g/day DHA for 10 weeks (n=74); fish-oil use on >=60 days in 1679 young men; fish-intake quartiles.
dose.too_much: Above ~3 g/day EPA+DHA raises bleeding risk; choose low-mercury fish.
dose.timeframe: 10-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Swap processed meat for fish: the fish-sperm association was strongest when fish replaced processed red meat.

factors.mechanism: DHA is a key structural lipid of sperm membranes; supplementation raised seminal antioxidant capacity. Paradoxically more PUFA means more oxidisable substrate, so benefit depends on adequate antioxidant status.
factors.interactions: Pairs with [nuts-walnuts-sperm] (plant omega-3) and [mediterranean-diet-sperm].
factors.caveats: Supplement trials are small; the Danish fish-oil study is cross-sectional; reviews note heterogeneity.

key_numbers.label: Total count, lowest vs highest fish quartile

factors.name: Tomatoes and lycopene
factors.headline: A placebo-controlled trial of 14 mg/day lycopene improved fast motility and morphology, but missed its primary endpoint; no SDF data.

dose.effective: About 14 mg lycopene/day, roughly half a cup of tomato sauce or passata (content varies by product); cooked tomato with some oil is better absorbed than raw.
dose.studied_range: 14 mg/day lactolycopene for 12 weeks in 60 healthy men.
dose.timeframe: 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Getting lycopene from food also brings other carotenoids and fibre.

factors.mechanism: Lycopene is a potent singlet-oxygen quencher concentrated in the testes and seminal fluid.
factors.interactions: Part of [mediterranean-diet-sperm]; included in the MOXI supplement (10 mg), which was null.
factors.caveats: Single small trial in healthy men; primary outcome (motile sperm concentration) not significant (p=0.058).

factors.name: Fruit and vegetables
factors.headline: Low-pesticide fruit and vegetables (2.8+ servings a day) are linked to much higher sperm counts; high-residue produce is not.

dose.effective: At least 3 servings/day; wash produce and favour lower-residue choices.
dose.studied_range: <1.1 to >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-residue produce.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Benefit is likely part of the overall dietary pattern.

factors.mechanism: Food-level vitamin C, folate, carotenoids and polyphenols support seminal antioxidant defences without the megadoses that cause reductive stress.
factors.interactions: See [pesticides-sperm] and [mediterranean-diet-sperm].
factors.caveats: Total fruit and vegetable intake was unrelated to semen in the same study; the finding depended on pesticide residue classification.

key_numbers.label: Higher total count, >=2.8 servings/day low-residue produce

factors.name: Processed meat (bacon, ham, hot dogs, deli meats)
factors.headline: Processed meat is the meat signal for sperm: men eating the most had fewer normal-shaped sperm (1.7 points) and, in young men, about 78 million fewer sperm per ejaculate. Unprocessed red meat was not linked to worse semen.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat (bacon, ham, sausages, deli meats) to less than one serving a week; replace with fish or legumes.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of intake in 155 clinic patients.
dose.too_much: Highest quartile associated with worse morphology.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.

factors.mechanism: Heme iron, nitrites and advanced glycation/lipoxidation products may increase oxidative stress; may also mark a Western diet.
factors.interactions: Replace with [fish-omega3-sperm] or unprocessed meat/poultry; see [unprocessed-red-meat-sperm].
factors.caveats: Observational only, small effects, and confounding by overall diet and abstinence time is possible (the young-men study noted heavy meat eaters also had shorter abstinence). The finding is specific to processed meat; see [unprocessed-red-meat-sperm].

key_numbers.label: Fewer normal forms, highest vs lowest quartile

factors.name: Sugar-sweetened beverages
factors.headline: Young men drinking 1.3+ sugary drinks a day had about 10 points lower progressive motility.

dose.effective: Under one sugary drink a week; water, unsweetened tea or coffee instead.
dose.studied_range: <0.2 to >=1.3 servings/day.
dose.too_much: >=1.3 servings/day associated with lower motility.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Caffeinated soft drinks also looked worse than coffee in reviews.

factors.mechanism: Glycaemic load drives insulin resistance, advanced glycation end-products and inflammation.
factors.interactions: Linked with [obesity-sperm].
factors.caveats: Cross-sectional, single semen sample; association only in lean men.

factors.name: Coffee and caffeine
factors.headline: Moderate coffee or tea does not clearly affect semen quality; caffeinated soft drinks and energy drinks look worse.

dose.effective: Up to about 2-3 cups of coffee per day appears fine.
dose.studied_range: 28 observational studies, nearly 20,000 men.
dose.too_much: Avoid large intakes from colas and energy drinks.
dose.notes: Some studies linked caffeine to sperm aneuploidy and DNA breaks, but findings are inconsistent.

factors.mechanism: Coffee polyphenols are antioxidant; caffeine effects on sperm DNA are uncertain.
factors.interactions: Separate from [sugary-drinks-sperm].
factors.caveats: Observational and inconsistent; residual confounding by smoking.

factors.name: Soy foods
factors.headline: Soy does not change male hormones in clinical trials and male soy intake was unrelated to IVF success; one small study linked very high intake to lower concentration.

dose.effective: Normal dietary amounts (1-2 servings/day of tofu, soy milk, edamame) are fine.
dose.studied_range: Up to the highest intake category in 99 clinic patients; 41 clinical studies of hormones.
dose.too_much: Very high intake (top of distribution) associated with 41 million/mL lower concentration in one study, mainly in overweight men.

factors.mechanism: Isoflavones are weak phytoestrogens; hormone-level trials show no feminising effect in men.
factors.interactions: Can replace [processed-meat-sperm] as protein.
factors.caveats: The negative association comes from one small cross-sectional study.

factors.name: Combination 'male fertility' antioxidant supplements
factors.headline: Cochrane finds possible benefit only from small, biased trials; the best-designed RCT (MOXI) showed no improvement in semen, DNA fragmentation or live birth.

dose.effective: No dose has proven benefit for live birth. If used, choose a modest-dose product (roughly vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, selenium 100-200 ug, zinc 15-25 mg, folate 400-1000 ug, CoQ10 100-200 mg, L-carnitine 1-2 g) for 3 months, not stacked products.
dose.studied_range: MOXI: vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.2 mg, L-carnitine 1000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1000 ug, lycopene 10 mg daily for 3-6 months. Cochrane: 20 different antioxidants in 90 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Stacking several products or megadoses risks reductive stress ([high-dose-antioxidant-reductive-stress]); antioxidants cause more mild GI upset (OR 2.70).
dose.timeframe: Trials use 3-6 months.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: counsel that supplements are of questionable clinical utility. EAU: insufficient evidence for widespread empirical use. Yet in a global survey 85.6% of reproductive specialists prescribed them.

factors.mechanism: Intended to scavenge seminal ROS and support antioxidant enzymes; only helpful if a man actually has oxidative stress and a deficiency.
factors.interactions: Not a substitute for removing the source of ROS ([smoking-sperm], [varicocele], [genital-tract-infection]). May blunt hormetic benefits of [exercise-moderate-sperm].
factors.caveats: Cochrane 2022: live birth OR 1.43 but very low certainty and null when high-risk-of-bias trials are removed; MOXI live birth was 15% vs 24% with placebo (not significant, small). A 6-month RCT in men with DFI >=25% also found no DFI change. Supplements may help a subgroup with proven oxidative stress, but no validated test identifies them.

key_numbers.label: Live birth OR (all trials, very low certainty)

factors.name: Folic acid + zinc
factors.headline: The largest male supplement trial (FAZST, 2370 couples) found folic acid plus zinc did nothing for semen or live birth, and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Not recommended for male fertility.
dose.studied_range: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg elemental zinc daily for 6 months.
dose.too_much: SDF 29.7% vs 27.2% with placebo (+2.4 points); more GI symptoms. Long-term zinc above ~40 mg/day can cause copper deficiency.
dose.timeframe: 6 months studied.
dose.notes: Correcting a genuine zinc or folate deficiency via diet is still sensible.

factors.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism and DNA methylation; zinc stabilises sperm chromatin and is an antioxidant enzyme cofactor. High doses did not help replete men.
factors.interactions: High-dose folate overlaps with [high-dose-antioxidant-reductive-stress] concerns.
factors.caveats: Population was general infertility patients, not selected for deficiency.

factors.name: Vitamins C and E
factors.headline: An uncontrolled study found 1 g vitamin C + 1 g vitamin E for 2 months lowered SDF and boosted the next ICSI's pregnancy rate, but controlled trials of similar mixes are null.

dose.effective: If used before ICSI for high SDF: about 500-1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E daily for 2-3 months, under medical advice.
dose.studied_range: 1 g C + 1 g E daily for 2 months (38 men).
dose.too_much: Vitamin C contributed to opening protamine disulphide bridges (sperm decondensation) in one study; vitamin E above 1000 mg/day raises bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: 2-3 months.
dose.notes: Both are in MOXI at lower doses, which was null.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin C is the main water-soluble antioxidant of seminal plasma; vitamin E protects PUFA-rich membranes from lipid peroxidation.
factors.interactions: See [male-antioxidant-combination] and [high-dose-antioxidant-reductive-stress].
factors.caveats: Greco 2005 was a before-after comparison after a failed cycle, so regression to the mean and cycle-to-cycle variation can explain much of the effect.

factors.name: Coenzyme Q10
factors.headline: CoQ10 at 200-300 mg/day modestly raises sperm motility and concentration, but there is no evidence it raises pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: 200 mg/day (ubiquinone or ubiquinol) with a fat-containing meal for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 200-300 mg/day for 3-6 months.
dose.too_much: Well tolerated; may interact with warfarin.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Men with low baseline motility and low seminal CoQ10 responded best.

factors.mechanism: Electron carrier in the mitochondrial electron transport chain and lipid-soluble antioxidant in sperm midpiece membranes.
factors.interactions: Common ingredient in [male-antioxidant-combination] products.
factors.caveats: Meta-analysis of 3 small RCTs; no live-birth data; SDF rarely measured.

factors.name: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine
factors.headline: Carnitines improve sperm motility and morphology in small trials, with no demonstrable effect on pregnancy; very high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: 1-2 g/day L-carnitine (often with 0.5-1 g acetyl-L-carnitine) for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 8 RCTs, mostly 2 g/day L-carnitine + 1 g acetyl-L-carnitine.
dose.too_much: In healthy mice, moderate-to-high carnitine doses caused severe sperm DNA fragmentation and lower pregnancy rates (reductive stress).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Can cause fishy body odour and GI upset; raises TMAO.

factors.mechanism: Transports fatty acids into mitochondria for sperm energy; antioxidant properties in the epididymis.
factors.interactions: Included in MOXI (1 g), which was null. See [high-dose-antioxidant-reductive-stress].
factors.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; pregnancy not improved.

factors.name: Selenium
factors.headline: Selenium helps motility mainly in men with low selenium status; little reason to supplement if diet is adequate.

dose.effective: About 100-200 ug/day only if intake is low (e.g. parts of Europe); 1-2 Brazil nuts provide a similar amount.
dose.studied_range: 3 months of selenium with or without vitamins A, C, E (69 men); MOXI used 200 ug.
dose.too_much: Do not exceed the US tolerable upper intake of 400 ug/day; chronic excess causes selenosis.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

factors.mechanism: Cofactor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4), which becomes a structural protein of the sperm midpiece and protects against lipid peroxidation.
factors.interactions: Part of [male-antioxidant-combination].
factors.caveats: Small, older trials; benefit limited to deficient men.

factors.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
factors.headline: NAC 600 mg/day for 3 months lowered SDF and improved motility in an uncontrolled study; no placebo-controlled live-birth data.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in 50 men with asthenoteratozoospermia.
dose.too_much: Higher doses add GI upset; no proven extra benefit.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

factors.mechanism: Cysteine donor for glutathione synthesis; also reported to induce Nrf2 target genes in sperm.
factors.interactions: Part of many combination products.
factors.caveats: Before-after design without placebo. Some widely cited NAC/selenium RCTs come from an author several of whose other papers have been retracted; they are not used here.

factors.name: Astaxanthin
factors.headline: One tiny trial (30 men) found 16 mg/day astaxanthin lowered seminal ROS and reported more pregnancies; never replicated at scale.

dose.effective: 16 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 16 mg/day, 3 months.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

factors.mechanism: Carotenoid that spans lipid bilayers and quenches singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals.
factors.interactions: Similar role to [tomatoes-lycopene-sperm].
factors.caveats: 11 vs 19 analysed men; pregnancy result very fragile; industry-supplied product.

factors.name: Vitamin D
factors.headline: In a 330-man RCT, high-dose vitamin D did not improve semen quality in men with low vitamin D, though live birth rose in a small oligozoospermic subgroup.

dose.effective: Correct deficiency (25OHD <50 nmol/L) for general health; not a sperm treatment.
dose.studied_range: 300,000 IU loading dose then 1400 IU/day plus 500 mg calcium for 150 days.
dose.too_much: Avoid chronic intake above 4000 IU/day without monitoring.
dose.timeframe: 150 days studied.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in testis and sperm; proposed effects on calcium signalling and inhibin B.
factors.caveats: The subgroup benefit is hypothesis-generating only.

factors.name: Megadose or stacked antioxidants ('reductive stress')
factors.headline: Too much antioxidant can loosen sperm chromatin: one study saw DFI fall 19% but decondensation rise 23%, and high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: Avoid taking several fertility products at once or doses well above the RDA (e.g. vitamin C >1 g, zinc >40 mg, folic acid >1 mg) without a specific indication.
dose.studied_range: Antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium for 90 days (human); dose-escalation of vitamin C, zinc, folate, carnitine (mice).
dose.too_much: This factor is the 'too much' end of [male-antioxidant-combination].
dose.timeframe: Over one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: FAZST's small SDF increase with 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc is consistent with this concern.

factors.mechanism: Sperm chromatin compaction depends on oxidative formation of protamine disulphide bridges in the epididymis, and capacitation needs a controlled ROS burst. Excess reductants (especially vitamin C) can reduce these disulphide bonds and blunt physiological ROS signalling.
factors.interactions: Opposes the benefits sought from [male-antioxidant-combination] and [vitamin-c-e-sperm]; also relevant to [l-carnitine-sperm].
factors.caveats: Human evidence is one small uncontrolled study plus indirect trial data; the mouse data may not transfer. Plausible but unproven.

factors.name: Unprocessed red meat (beef, pork, lamb)
factors.headline: Not linked to worse semen quality. In young US men unprocessed red meat showed no association with any semen measure, and a Chinese case-control study linked higher unprocessed meat intake to lower odds of poor motility (OR 0.61). The negative meat signal for sperm comes from processed meat.

dose.effective: No evidence-based target. Normal portions of unprocessed red meat are compatible with sperm health; cooking method may matter more than the meat itself.
dose.studied_range: Food-frequency quartiles/tertiles of habitual intake.
dose.timeframe: ~2-3 months (one spermatogenic cycle) for any dietary change to show in semen.
dose.notes: Red meat is a dense source of zinc, vitamin B12, iron and carnitine, which sperm production needs. That matters most if intake is low (e.g. restrictive diets). In men who were not deficient, adding 30 mg/day zinc (with folic acid) did not improve semen or live birth in the large FAZST trial.

factors.mechanism: No direct human evidence that red meat improves spermatogenesis or spermiogenesis. The plausible route is nutrient supply (zinc, B12, iron, carnitine) in people with low intake. The oxidative concerns that apply to processed meat (nitrites, preformed N-nitroso compounds) do not apply to fresh meat, while high-heat or stir-fry cooking can add oxidized products.
factors.interactions: Contrast with [processed-meat-sperm]. High-heat cooking was associated with worse motility in the case-control study. Extra zinc on top of an adequate diet did not help ([folate-zinc-sperm]).
factors.caveats: Two observational studies with different populations; no trials. The case-control result could reflect overall diet or recall bias. Absence of harm is not proof of benefit.

factors.name: Curcumin supplements for sperm quality
factors.headline: One small Iranian RCT (56 completers) found 80 mg/day nanomicelle curcumin for 10 weeks improved sperm count, concentration and motility plus seminal-redox and inflammation markers; there are no human data on DNA fragmentation, varicocele, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: 80 mg/day curcumin as nanomicelle for 10 weeks in the only RCT.
dose.studied_range: 80 mg/day (single human RCT); animal varicocele studies used 4-100 mg/kg.
dose.too_much: Not established for sperm. In vitro, curcumin added directly to sperm blocks motility and capacitation in a concentration-dependent way (it has been studied as a vaginal contraceptive), although such concentrations are not reached in semen after oral dosing. General supplement risks (liver injury, drug interactions) apply.
dose.timeframe: At least one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days); the RCT ran 10 weeks.
dose.notes: Human DNA-fragmentation benefits come only from adding curcumin to freezing medium in the lab (cryopreservation), not from oral use. Varicocele data are from rats only (mechanistic).

factors.mechanism: Proposed: lowering seminal lipid peroxidation (MDA) and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-a, CRP) and Nrf2-driven antioxidant enzymes in testis. Human mechanistic support is limited to blood TAC/MDA changes in one trial.
factors.interactions: Likely overlaps with other antioxidant approaches such as [n-acetylcysteine]; no head-to-head or combination trials. Redundant with [sulforaphane-supplements] on the Nrf2 axis (inference). Not comparable to culinary [turmeric-curcumin].
factors.caveats: A single small trial from one country, without pregnancy outcomes, cannot support a recommendation; it does not show more pregnancies. The in-vitro anti-motility effect argues against assuming 'more is better'. Check for publication bias as further Iranian trials appear.

key_numbers.label: Dose in the only human RCT
Curcumin in freezing medium that reduced post-thaw DNA fragmentation

factors.name: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for sperm quality
factors.headline: No human trial has tested sulforaphane or broccoli sprouts on sperm DNA fragmentation, motility or fertility; protection is shown only in rodents exposed to toxins, diabetes or high-fat diets and in human sperm treated in the lab.

dose.effective: Unknown for sperm. General-health doses (30-70 g fresh sprouts, or 40-150 µmol sulforaphane/day) are the only human-tested amounts.
dose.studied_range: Rodents: injected or oral sulforaphane for weeks to months; in vitro: 5 µM added to human semen before freezing.
dose.too_much: Not established; in cell culture sulforaphane becomes cytotoxic above about 10-15 µM, far above blood levels from food.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (about 74 days) would be needed to see any effect.
dose.notes: The in vitro cryopreservation result applies to sperm-freezing media, not to eating broccoli.

factors.mechanism: Nrf2-driven antioxidant genes in testis, AMPK-dependent relief of ER stress in sperm, and reduced testicular apoptosis in diabetic or toxin-exposed animals.
factors.interactions: Same redundancy considerations as [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]; no data on combining with other sperm antioxidants such as [n-acetylcysteine].
factors.caveats: All evidence is animal or in vitro; rodent models used toxic exposures (phthalates, diabetes, high-fat diet) and often injected doses. Do not expect measurable improvement in semen analysis from broccoli in healthy men.

factors.name: Pomegranate fruit extract (with galangal)
factors.headline: In one 70-man RCT, pomegranate-fruit extract plus galangal tablets for 3 months raised the total number of motile sperm by 62%, vs 20% on placebo; it has not been replicated and pregnancy was not measured.

dose.effective: Daily standardised pomegranate-extract plus galangal tablets (Punalpin) for 3 months.
dose.studied_range: 3 months.
dose.timeframe: About 3 months (one spermatogenic cycle plus transit).
dose.notes: The extract was standardised for punicalagins, punicalin and ellagic acid; effect of pomegranate alone is unknown.

factors.mechanism: Not established in humans; candidates are ellagitannin-derived metabolites (urolithins, metabotype-dependent) and galangal's acetoxychavicol acetate.
factors.interactions: Overlaps [male-antioxidant-combination]. Urolithin production varies by metabotype (see [urolithin-a]).
factors.caveats: Single trial; participants were men whose semen did not meet sperm-bank standards, not infertile couples; no pregnancy or DNA-fragmentation outcomes.

key_numbers.label: Total motile sperm increase, active vs placebo

factors.name: Resveratrol (multivitamin-based) for sperm
factors.headline: The only human data are an uncontrolled 20-man pilot of a multivitamin with 150 mg/day resveratrol, which reported motility rising from 48% to 59%; with no placebo group the effect cannot be attributed to resveratrol.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: 150 mg/day resveratrol within a multivitamin for 3-6 months.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.

factors.mechanism: Proposed SIRT1 and mitochondrial effects in sperm, from animal work.
factors.interactions: Overlaps [male-antioxidant-combination]; see [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements] for general resveratrol evidence.
factors.caveats: Uncontrolled, small, multi-ingredient, no pregnancy outcomes; regression to the mean is likely.

factors.name: Ketogenic diet (male fertility)
factors.headline: In men with obesity, very-low-calorie ketogenic diets raised total testosterone by ~6.75 nmol/L (normocaloric keto by ~1 nmol/L), in proportion to weight lost. No human trial has measured semen quality on keto; the only semen data are from obese mice.

dose.effective: Weight loss via a supervised very-low-calorie ketogenic diet (8-14 weeks) in men with obesity-related low testosterone, then a sustainable diet.
dose.studied_range: 7 studies, 230 participants; mostly uncontrolled before-after designs of 8-14 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid weight loss and very-low-calorie protocols need medical supervision. LDL may rise in lean men.
dose.timeframe: Testosterone changes within 8-12 weeks; any semen effect would need at least one ~74-day spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Probably a weight-loss effect rather than a ketone effect. Higher-fat diets keep testosterone a little higher than low-fat diets (SMD ~0.38), independent of keto.

factors.mechanism: Weight loss lowers aromatase activity and insulin resistance, which releases hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal suppression. In obese mice an MCT-based ketogenic diet lowered testicular lipid peroxidation and raised glutathione peroxidase.
factors.interactions: Essentially a subset of [weight-loss-sperm] / [obesity-sperm]. General effects are under [ketogenic-diet].
factors.caveats: No controlled human semen data. The testosterone meta-analysis pools mostly uncontrolled studies, and the gains track weight loss and age. The animal data compare keto with a high-fat high-cholesterol obesogenic diet, not with a healthy diet.

factors.name: Fasting and sperm (Ramadan, TRE, multi-day fasts)
factors.headline: No trial shows fasting improves sperm; a 48-h fast cut LH by ~64% and lowered testosterone, 16:8 TRE lowered testosterone in trained men, and a retrospective IVF study found lower progressive motility (30% vs 38%) in samples produced during Ramadan.

dose.effective: None established. If overweight, the benefit comes from losing weight by any method; daily 12-14 h overnight fasts appear harmless.
dose.studied_range: 48-h fasts, 8 weeks of 16:8 TRE, Ramadan (dawn-to-sunset fasting for a month), three 5-day FMD cycles.
dose.too_much: Multi-day fasts suppress the reproductive axis within 48 h; avoid them during the ~74-day window before conception attempts or semen analysis.
dose.timeframe: Hormone changes within 48 h; semen effects would need one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days).
dose.notes: Ramadan meta-analysis found no average change in testosterone, LH or FSH, so daily dawn-to-dusk fasting is probably neutral for hormones.

factors.mechanism: Acute energy deficit slows hypothalamic GnRH/LH pulsatility and lowers testosterone and IGF-1; dehydration and circadian disruption during Ramadan may affect semen volume and motility.
factors.interactions: Weight loss in men with obesity improves semen quality; see [weight-loss-sperm] and [obesity-sperm]. Poor sleep during late-night eating periods overlaps with [poor-sleep-sperm].
factors.caveats: Human sperm data are a 21-man 1986 study, a 97-man retrospective IVF cohort, and an 18-man FMD pilot. Rodent studies of fasting and sperm are not transferable.

factors.name: Chronic high-volume endurance training and low testosterone (exercise-hypogonadal male condition)
factors.headline: Men with years of very high endurance volumes (e.g. ~100+ km/week running, elite triathlon) can develop persistently low testosterone without raised LH, and small studies show lower motility, more immature sperm and high DNA fragmentation (~20% in elite triathletes), though changes rarely fall below WHO thresholds.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and training very high volumes, cut back toward moderate volumes for about 3 months, eat enough to match training (avoid low energy availability), and keep cycling under about 5 h/week.
dose.studied_range: High-mileage runners ~108 km/week vs ~54 km/week vs sedentary; elite triathletes in championship preparation; endurance athletes in cross-sectional and short training studies (280 athletes across 13 studies).
dose.too_much: Hormonal and semen changes appeared at high-mileage running (~100+ km/week) and elite triathlon training, not at moderate volumes.
dose.timeframe: Spermatogenesis takes ~74 days, so allow about 3 months after reducing load; testosterone recovers when energy balance and load normalise, sometimes over months.
dose.notes: Recreational activity is associated with equal or better semen quality ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]). Men with low testosterone should not self-treat with testosterone, which shuts down sperm production ([testosterone-anabolic-steroids]).

factors.mechanism: Chronic training load and low energy availability suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulses (functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), lowering testosterone; high cortisol, systemic and seminal inflammation (more round cells/leukocytes), scrotal heat and oxidative stress during heavy training may add sperm DNA damage.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [cycling] (saddle pressure, heat) and [overtraining-ultraendurance]; the female counterpart is [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]. Adequate sleep ([short-sleep]) and energy intake support recovery.
factors.caveats: Evidence is small, cross-sectional and mostly in elite athletes; whether low testosterone reflects dysfunction or an adaptive readjustment is debated, and few studies measure fertility (pregnancy) outcomes.
factors.debate: Hackney's group describes a persistent 'exercise-hypogonadal male condition' with possible spermatogenesis effects [exr-lane2019, exr-hackney2008], supported by lower testosterone and semen quality in high-mileage runners [exr-desouza1994], high DNA fragmentation in elite triathletes [exr-vaamonde2018], and lower libido at the highest training loads [exr-hackney2017]; the IOC REDs consensus and a review of male runners link it to low energy availability [exr-mountjoy2023, exr-cupka2023]. But Hackney himself argues some cases may be adaptive rather than pathological [exr-hackney2020]; a systematic review found semen changes in endurance athletes rarely clinically relevant [exr-aerts2024]; a meta-analysis found most activity has no major semen effect, with harm limited to elite levels [exr-ibanezperez2019]; and in large preconception cohorts male vigorous activity was not consistently associated with couples' fecundability [exr-wise2025].

factors.name: Microplastics in testis and semen
factors.headline: Plastic particles have been reported in human testes (Py-GC/MS, mean 328 ug/g in 23 men) and in most semen samples (a few particles each by Raman or infrared), with hints of lower motility in studies of 40-45 men, but the testis method is disputed and there are no human data on sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: No proven intervention; use the general exposure steps in [microplastics] (don't heat food in plastic, prefer tap over bottled water where safe).
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional measurements in 6-45 men per study.
dose.timeframe: Unknown; any effect on sperm would take at least one ~74-day spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Different methods give incompatible numbers: Py-GC/MS reports mass (ug/g), spectroscopy counts a handful of particles.

factors.mechanism: In rodents, polystyrene micro/nanoplastics cross the blood-testis barrier, raise testicular ROS and inflammation and reduce sperm count and motility; human mechanistic data are lacking.
factors.interactions: Plastic particles carry phthalates and bisphenols ([plastics-chemicals]), which are hard to separate from particle effects.
factors.caveats: Tiny samples, no exposure gradient, no contamination-proof designs; motility differences were borderline (p=0.056) or between polymer types rather than exposed vs unexposed.
factors.debate: Presence: Py-GC/MS found plastic in every human testis [env-hu2024] and spectroscopy found particles in semen [env-montano2023, env-li2024, env-zhao2023, env-guo2025]. A published comment argued the testis study lacked blanks, controls and method validation [env-uppu2025]; the authors defended their digestion method but limited future work to 6 reliable polymers [env-hu2025]. Py-GC/MS polyethylene and PVC values in biological samples are vulnerable to false positives [env-rauert2025]. Harm: animal studies frequently report testicular damage but often lack dose and particle characterization [env-due2026].

factors.name: PFAS and sperm
factors.headline: Pooled data link PFAS to slightly lower progressive motility and more sperm DNA fragmentation (r = 0.14 across 14 studies), but the effects are small, individual studies disagree, and a 604-man study found no consistent SDF effect.

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention tested. If exposure is likely, see [pfas] for testing and exposure reduction.
dose.studied_range: General-population serum PFOS ~5-25 ng/mL; occupational groups higher.
dose.too_much: NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased general health risk (not a fertility-specific threshold).
dose.timeframe: PFAS half-lives are years, so serum (and any sperm effect) changes slowly.
dose.notes: Effect sizes are correlations of about 0.06-0.14, i.e. small at the individual level.

factors.mechanism: PFAS reach the testis and seminal plasma; in animals they lower testosterone, disrupt Sertoli and Leydig cells and raise oxidative stress.
factors.interactions: Occurs alongside other persistent pollutants (PCBs, organochlorines) that confound associations; see [plastics-chemicals] for short-lived endocrine disruptors.
factors.caveats: Cross-sectional, single-sample designs; many congener-by-endpoint tests invite chance findings.
factors.debate: A 2026 meta-analysis found consistent inverse links with motility and DNA integrity [env-dinisio2026] and an earlier one found PFOA/PFNA linked to lower progressive motility [env-wangh2023a]; Danish young men with high PFOS+PFOA had fewer normal sperm [env-joensen2009]. Against this, a 604-man study found no consistent link with SCSA DNA fragmentation [env-specht2012], the LIFE study found associations in varying directions [env-louis2015], and a systematic review found little consistent evidence in men [env-bach2016].

factors.name: Personal lubricants and sperm
factors.headline: In the lab, many lubricants (K-Y, Astroglide, olive oil, saliva) cut sperm motility and some raise DNA fragmentation, while isotonic 'sperm-friendly' gels (e.g. Pre-Seed) do not; yet in two cohorts (6,467 and 296 women) lubricant use did not lower the chance of conceiving.

dose.effective: For natural conception, lubricant choice appears not to matter in cohort data; if wanted, pick an isotonic 'fertility-friendly' product. For semen collection (semen analysis, IUI, IVF), use none or a clinic-approved isotonic lubricant (Pre-Seed did not change motility, ROS or DNA damage in a crossover trial).
dose.studied_range: In vitro lubricant concentrations of 5-12.5% in semen for 10 min to 4 h; cohorts of natural conception attempts.
dose.timeframe: In vitro motility falls within 10-30 minutes of contact.
dose.notes: Saliva is one of the worst performers in vitro. Paraben preservatives at lubricant concentrations raised sperm ROS in vitro.

factors.mechanism: Hyperosmolar, acidic or viscous gels and preservatives (parabens, glycerol) impair motility and can raise mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA adducts in vitro; isotonic, pH-matched gels avoid this.
factors.interactions: Relevant mainly when sperm quality is already marginal or for samples collected for assisted reproduction.
factors.caveats: In vitro tests expose washed sperm to lubricant directly, unlike intercourse where most sperm enter cervical mucus quickly. Cohort data rely on self-reported lubricant type; no randomized fertility trial exists.
factors.debate: Lab studies show many lubricants impair motility or chromatin [env-anderson1998, env-agarwal2008, env-tulandi1982, env-mackenzie2019], with 'sperm-friendly' products performing best [env-mowat2014, env-tomlinson2023] and parabens adding oxidative stress [env-samarasinghe2018]. Real-world data disagree with the lab: no lubricant type reduced fecundability in a 6,467-woman cohort [env-mcinerney2018] or in a smaller diary study [env-steiner2012]. Reviews conclude the question is unresolved and that a randomized trial is needed [env-mesen2014, env-gumerova2024].

key_numbers.label: Fecundability ratio, any lubricant in fertile window

factors.name: SSRIs (antidepressants) and sperm DNA
factors.headline: In 35 healthy men, 4 weeks of paroxetine raised sperm DNA fragmentation from 13.8% to 30.3% (abnormal in 50% of men vs 9.7% before) with a normal standard semen analysis; small sertraline and escitalopram studies point the same way and effects appear reversible.

dose.effective: Effects seen at standard antidepressant or premature-ejaculation doses: paroxetine (4 weeks), sertraline 50 mg/day (3 months), escitalopram 10 mg/day (12 weeks).
dose.studied_range: Single-arm or small controlled studies of 25-60 men, 4-12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No dose threshold established; a sperm DNA fragmentation test (rather than a routine semen analysis) is what detects the change.
dose.timeframe: DNA fragmentation rose within 4 weeks; reversal after stopping is expected over about one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days) but timing data are limited.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Untreated depression also lowers couple fertility; men trying to conceive who take SSRIs can discuss a DNA fragmentation test, timing, or alternatives with the prescriber rather than stopping.

factors.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms include serotonin effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and epididymal transit, and direct effects on sperm membranes and chromatin; DNA fragmentation without changes in count or motility suggests a post-testicular or chromatin-packaging effect [med-tanrikut2010, med-beeder2020].
factors.interactions: Untreated [psychological-stress] and depression are themselves linked to lower fertility. Ejaculatory delay on SSRIs may lengthen abstinence; see [short-abstinence]. Not known whether [male-antioxidant-combination] offsets the effect.
factors.caveats: Studies are small, mostly uncontrolled, and many are in men treated for premature ejaculation. No study shows lower live-birth rates from paternal SSRI use.
factors.debate: Harm: paroxetine [med-tanrikut2010], escitalopram [med-koyuncu2011] and sertraline (vs behavioural therapy) [med-akasheh2014] all worsened sperm measures, and reviews conclude SSRIs can harm semen quality reversibly [med-beeder2020]. Caution: a frequently cited large study [med-safarinejad2008] is under a 2023 Expression of Concern; a systematic review rated most male studies poor quality [med-sylvester2019]; and in a preconception cohort, male depression rather than medication explained most of a weak fecundability association [med-yland2022], with active depression in men linked to lower conception [med-evanshoeker2018].

factors.name: Finasteride & dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors)
factors.headline: Hair-loss-dose finasteride (1 mg) left semen unchanged in 181 young men, but prostate doses (finasteride 5 mg, dutasteride 0.5 mg) cut total sperm count about 30%, and subfertile men on finasteride saw counts rise on average 11.6-fold after stopping.

dose.effective: Finasteride 1 mg/day (hair loss) or 5 mg/day (prostate); dutasteride 0.5 mg/day.
dose.studied_range: Finasteride 1 mg/day for 48 weeks (RCT); finasteride 5 mg and dutasteride 0.5 mg for 1 year (RCT); mean 1 mg/day for ~57 months (subfertile men).
dose.too_much: Prostate doses and dutasteride have larger effects (semen volume -29.7% on dutasteride); men who are already oligospermic appear most vulnerable even at 1 mg.
dose.timeframe: Counts fell by 26 weeks; recovery after stopping over months (one spermatogenic cycle is ~74 days).
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men with low counts who are trying to conceive and use finasteride for hair loss can ask about pausing it; a repeat semen analysis about 3 months after stopping shows whether it was a factor.

factors.mechanism: Blocking conversion of testosterone to DHT (by 73% with finasteride 5 mg and 94% with dutasteride) reduces prostate and seminal-vesicle secretions and modestly impairs epididymal sperm maturation; testosterone itself rises slightly [med-amory2007].
factors.interactions: Unlike [testosterone-anabolic-steroids], 5-ARIs do not shut down LH/FSH. Often used alongside [alpha-blockers-sperm] for prostate enlargement, which adds ejaculatory problems.
factors.caveats: The dramatic recovery data come from 27 men who presented with infertility, a selected group; healthy men on 1 mg show no average change.
factors.debate: In healthy young men, 1 mg finasteride did not affect spermatogenesis [med-overstreet1999]; in subfertile men on similar doses, counts rose sharply after stopping [med-samplaski2013], suggesting a vulnerable subgroup. Prostate doses produced mild, mostly reversible falls [med-amory2007].
