factors.name: Opioid painkillers & methadone
factors.headline: Regular opioid use, including methadone, lowers testosterone by about 165 ng/dL in men, and reviews report lower semen quality and higher sperm DNA fragmentation; direct human semen studies are few and low quality.

dose.effective: Effects described with regular (daily) use of any opioid, including maintenance methadone.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional and cohort studies of chronic users; no dose-response trials.
dose.too_much: Higher doses and long-acting opioids appear worse; tramadol and tapentadol may cause less suppression.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal suppression develops with regular use; semen recovery after tapering is expected over months but is poorly studied.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Never stop opioids or methadone abruptly; tapering or switching must be supervised. Men on opioids with low testosterone who want children should not be treated with testosterone, which further suppresses sperm production.

factors.mechanism: Opioids suppress hypothalamic GnRH and hence LH and testosterone, increase aromatase, and act on opioid receptors in the testis and on sperm themselves [med-drobnis2017, med-bawor2015].
factors.interactions: Testosterone replacement ([testosterone-anabolic-steroids]) for opioid-induced low testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis; [glp1-agonists] raised testosterone without suppressing LH/FSH in obese men, though not studied in opioid users. [cannabis] is covered separately.
factors.caveats: Opioid users differ from controls in smoking, illness and other drug use, so semen findings are heavily confounded.
factors.debate: The testosterone effect is consistent across 17 studies, though heterogeneous and low quality [med-bawor2015]; the semen and DNA-fragmentation effects rest mainly on narrative review of small studies [med-drobnis2017]. No published study was found arguing opioids are harmless to sperm; the debate is about magnitude and reversibility.

key_numbers.label: Testosterone difference, opioid users vs controls

factors.name: Sulfasalazine & methotrexate (bowel and arthritis drugs)
factors.headline: Sulfasalazine (2-4 g/day) reliably but reversibly damages sperm, with pregnancies typically about 2.5 months after switching; low-dose methotrexate showed no change in semen or sperm DNA fragmentation and no excess birth defects in 127 children of exposed fathers.

dose.effective: Sulfasalazine 2-4 g/day; low-dose weekly methotrexate as used in arthritis, psoriasis and IBD.
dose.studied_range: Sulfasalazine 2-4 g/day for >2 months; methotrexate in 20 men followed prospectively and 127 Danish births.
dose.too_much: Sulfasalazine at any therapeutic dose for over 2 months; high-dose methotrexate as chemotherapy is a different exposure (see chemo-radiation).
dose.timeframe: Sulfasalazine effects reverse within about 2-3 months of switching; methotrexate data cover the 90 days before conception.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men on sulfasalazine who are trying to conceive can ask about switching to mesalazine or another agent; the ACR guideline supports continuing low-dose methotrexate in men planning conception.

factors.mechanism: The sulphapyridine part of sulfasalazine is toxic to maturing sperm late in their development (rat data show the same effect with sulphapyridine but not 5-aminosalicylic acid) [med-omorain1984]. Methotrexate barely accumulates in sperm because of low folylpolyglutamate synthetase activity [med-perezgarcia2023].
factors.interactions: Underlying inflammatory disease ([chronic-inflammation]) can itself affect fertility; high-dose cytotoxic treatment belongs under [chemo-radiation]. Folate status ([folate-zinc]) is relevant for methotrexate users.
factors.caveats: Sulfasalazine data are older and small but consistent. Methotrexate data come from 20 men and registry births; high-dose regimens are not covered.
factors.debate: Older advice to stop methotrexate 3 months before conception is contested by a Danish registry (aOR 1.01 for malformations) [med-eck2017] and a prospective semen study [med-perezgarcia2023]; reviews still describe its sperm effect as uncertain and note animal testicular toxicity [med-perezgarcia2020, med-banerjee2019]. For sulfasalazine there is no real disagreement: men on it have lower counts and motility than men on mesalazine [med-banerjee2019, med-toovey1981].

factors.name: Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin) and ejaculation
factors.headline: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg/day cut ejaculate volume by 2.4 mL and caused complete anejaculation in 35% of healthy men, and 95% of sexually active silodosin users reported ejaculatory disorder; alfuzosin had no such effect.

dose.effective: Tamsulosin 0.4-0.8 mg/day; silodosin 8 mg/day (typical prostate doses).
dose.studied_range: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg/day vs alfuzosin vs placebo (healthy volunteers); silodosin in 91 men with BPH.
dose.too_much: Higher tamsulosin doses and silodosin have the strongest effect.
dose.timeframe: Immediate and reversible on stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men trying to conceive who take these drugs can ask about an alternative (alfuzosin did not affect ejaculation in the healthy-volunteer trial) or timing.

factors.mechanism: Alpha-1A blockade relaxes the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and bladder neck, reducing emission of semen; the tamsulosin trial found this was not explained by retrograde ejaculation [med-hellstrom2006]. This is a mechanical, not a redox, effect.
factors.interactions: Often combined with [finasteride-sperm] (5-ARIs) for prostate enlargement, which also lowers semen volume.
factors.caveats: Ejaculate volume and anejaculation matter for natural conception; sperm production itself is not shown to be harmed.
factors.debate: No substantive published debate found on the effect itself; the size differs by drug, with tamsulosin and silodosin affecting most men and alfuzosin none in a head-to-head trial [med-hellstrom2006, med-sakata2012].

factors.name: Advanced sperm selection for ICSI (PICSI/hyaluronan, MACS, microfluidics, IMSI)
factors.headline: Selecting 'better' sperm lowers measured DNA fragmentation in the dish but has not raised live birth: PICSI in 2772 couples gave 27.4% vs 25.2% (NS), MACS and microfluidics trials are small and conflicting; HFEA rates PICSI black and SDF-guided selection grey.

dose.effective: Not routinely recommended (ESHRE); microfluidics 'can be considered'. If SDF is high, cheaper first steps are short abstinence and fixing causes.
dose.studied_range: Hyaluronan binding (PICSI), annexin-V magnetic beads (MACS), microfluidic chips, high-magnification morphology (IMSI).
dose.too_much: Extra cost per cycle; no safety signal.
dose.timeframe: Lab step on the day of ICSI.
dose.notes: Cochrane 2026: hyaluronan selection probably slightly reduces miscarriage (RR 0.59, moderate certainty), a secondary outcome.

factors.mechanism: Mature sperm with intact chromatin bind hyaluronan; apoptotic sperm expose phosphatidylserine (removed by MACS); microfluidic channels select motile sperm without the ROS burst of centrifugation. All aim to deliver sperm with less oxidative DNA damage to the egg.
factors.interactions: Alternatives for high SDF: [short-abstinence], [varicocele] repair, [testicular-sperm-icsi]; the egg's repair capacity falls with [maternal-age], so effects might differ by female age.
factors.caveats: Lower DFI in the prepared sample does not translate into live births in trials so far.
factors.debate: A small single-centre RCT reported higher live birth with a microfluidic chip (46.8% vs 25%) [fer-aydin2022], but a 2026 RCT found lower DFI without better live birth [fer-huong2026]; MACS RCTs were null [fer-romany2014, fer-mantravadi2024]. HABSelect was null for live birth [fer-miller2019], while Cochrane 2026 finds a probable miscarriage reduction with hyaluronan selection [fer-garg2026]. ESHRE: not routine, microfluidics 'can be considered' [fer-eshre2023addons]; HFEA: PICSI black, SDF-guided selection grey [fer-hfea2026, fer-hfea2026sdf].

key_numbers.label: Term live birth, PICSI vs ICSI (HABSelect)

factors.name: ICSI when sperm are normal (non-male-factor ICSI)
factors.headline: With normal sperm count and motility, ICSI did not beat conventional IVF in a 1064-couple Lancet RCT (live birth 35% vs 31%, NS; fertilisation failure 5% vs 6%), yet US registry data show two-thirds of non-male-factor cycles use it; ESHRE and ASRM advise against routine use.

dose.effective: Use conventional IVF when semen is normal; reserve ICSI for male factor, prior fertilisation failure, PGT cycles or very few eggs.
dose.studied_range: Sibling and randomised comparisons with WHO-normal semen.
dose.too_much: Extra cost and lab time; skips natural sperm selection at the egg's surface.
dose.timeframe: Fertilisation day.
dose.notes: Distinct from ICSI for genuine male factor, where it is the standard of care.

factors.mechanism: ICSI bypasses sperm binding and penetration; it rescues fertilisation when sperm cannot do this, but adds nothing when they can.
factors.interactions: Often combined with [sperm-selection-icsi-sperm]; high SDF is not by itself an indication for ICSI over IVF.
factors.caveats: Observational data even suggest slightly lower live birth with ICSI in non-male-factor cycles, but confounding is likely.
factors.debate: Some clinicians use ICSI routinely to avoid the small risk of total fertilisation failure; the Dang RCT found no difference in failure or live birth [fer-dang2021], and registry data found no benefit and slightly lower live birth (aRR 0.95) [fer-boulet2015]. ASRM and ESHRE advise against routine use [fer-asrm2020icsi, fer-eshre2023addons].

mechanisms.name: Why sperm are uniquely vulnerable
mechanisms.description: Sperm membranes are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids such as DHA, which are easily peroxidised. During maturation sperm shed almost all cytoplasm, so they carry very little superoxide dismutase, catalase or glutathione peroxidase and rely on seminal plasma for protection. They are transcriptionally silent and have only the first enzyme of base excision repair (OGG1), so oxidised bases are excised but the gaps cannot be filled.

mechanisms.name: Aitken's two-step hypothesis of sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Step 1: defective spermiogenesis leaves sperm with poor histone-to-protamine replacement, retained cytoplasm and loose chromatin. Step 2: oxidative stress (from the sperm's own mitochondria, from leukocytes, or from heat and toxicants) attacks this vulnerable DNA, forming 8-OHdG; OGG1 excises the lesion, leaving abasic sites that break into the strand breaks measured as SDF.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial ROS and apoptosis in sperm
mechanisms.description: Stressed or defective sperm leak electrons at mitochondrial complex I, producing superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; this triggers a truncated apoptotic cascade. Hydrogen peroxide from the midpiece crosses into the nucleus and damages DNA, while lipid peroxidation products (e.g. 4-hydroxynonenal) further poison mitochondria in a self-propagating loop.

mechanisms.name: Leukocyte NADPH oxidase
mechanisms.description: Activated neutrophils and macrophages in semen generate superoxide via NOX2 at far higher rates than sperm; infection and inflammation therefore produce oxidative bursts that overwhelm seminal antioxidants.

mechanisms.name: Oocyte repair of paternal DNA damage
mechanisms.description: After fertilisation the oocyte must complete base excision repair of the sperm's oxidised DNA before the first S-phase; unrepaired or misrepaired lesions become mutations present in every cell of the embryo. This repair capacity is limited and appears to fall with maternal age, which is why high SDF hurts ICSI outcomes mostly in women over 40.

mechanisms.name: Scrotal thermoregulation
mechanisms.description: Spermatogenesis needs a testicular temperature about 2-4 C below core. Heat disrupts protamination and mitochondrial function in developing germ cells and induces apoptosis, effects that appear 2-3 months later and reverse within about 3-6 months of removing the heat.

mechanisms.name: Reductive stress and chromatin compaction
mechanisms.description: Some ROS are needed: protamine disulphide bridges form oxidatively during epididymal transit, and capacitation needs a controlled oxidative burst. Large antioxidant doses can reduce these bonds and impair compaction, a proposed reason why antioxidant trials are inconsistent.

mechanisms.name: Spermatogenesis timeline
mechanisms.description: The textbook duration of spermatogenesis is about 74 days, based on 1960s labelling studies. Direct isotope labelling found new sperm first reaching the ejaculate about 64 days (range 42-76) after they started forming, including epididymal transit. Changes made today therefore start to show in about 2 months and are fully reflected after about 3 months.

mechanisms.name: What high sperm DNA fragmentation does clinically
mechanisms.description: High SDF is associated with longer time to natural pregnancy (fecundability falls as SCSA abnormal sperm rise, becoming small above 30-40%), about double the miscarriage risk (RR 2.16), higher SDF in partners of women with recurrent pregnancy loss (+11.9 points), and lower clinical pregnancy and live birth after IVF and, to a lesser extent, ICSI. Double-strand breaks may matter most for miscarriage. Associations are consistent but heterogeneous, and SDF predicts outcomes imperfectly.

mechanisms.name: Sperm DNA fragmentation and oxidative stress tests
mechanisms.description: SCSA (flow cytometry after acid denaturation; DFI, classic cut-off 25-30%), TUNEL (labels strand-break ends; flow cut-off about 17-20%), SCD/Halo (halo size after protein removal; ~20-30%) and Comet (single-cell electrophoresis; alkaline detects single- and double-strand breaks, neutral mainly double-strand). Expert guidelines use thresholds near 20% (about 26% for alkaline Comet). ASRM (2013) and AUA/ASRM (2020/2024) do not recommend SDF in the initial work-up but do for recurrent pregnancy loss; EAU recommends it for recurrent pregnancy loss, ART failure and unexplained infertility. MiOXSYS ORP is quick but its normalisation to sperm concentration makes it highly sensitive and poorly specific (40.6%), and EAU advises against routine ROS testing.

references.title: Oxidative stress and male reproductive health
references.finding: Sperm carry only OGG1, the first enzyme of base excision repair; the oocyte must finish repairing oxidised bases before the first S-phase, and errors become mutations in every cell of the embryo.

references.finding: Sperm are vulnerable because their membranes are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids and they have almost no cytoplasm for antioxidant enzymes; stressed sperm default to an apoptotic pathway with mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA damage.

references.authors: Aitken RJ, Lewis SEM

references.authors: Aitken RJ
references.title: Male reproductive ageing: a radical road to ruin
references.finding: Paternal ageing brings more sperm DNA damage, epigenetic change in the germ line and a higher mutational load in offspring.

references.authors: Tharakan T, Bettocchi C, Carvalho J, et al.

references.finding: EAU consultation guide on when to test SDF and on the still-experimental use of testicular sperm for ICSI in nonazoospermic men.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Cho CL, Majzoub A, et al.
references.title: The Society for Translational Medicine: clinical practice guidelines for sperm DNA fragmentation testing in male infertility
references.finding: Society for Translational Medicine guideline: test SDF in clinical varicocele with borderline semen, recurrent pregnancy loss, ART failure, unexplained infertility and men with lifestyle risk factors.

references.authors: Cho CL, Agarwal A, Majzoub A, et al.
references.title: Clinical utility of sperm DNA fragmentation testing: concise practice recommendations
references.finding: Concise expert practice recommendations on the clinical scenarios where SDF testing changes management.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Farkouh A, Parekh N, et al.
references.title: Sperm DNA Fragmentation: A Critical Assessment of Clinical Practice Guidelines
references.finding: Compares the Agarwal and Esteves SDF guidelines; both use thresholds around 20% for TUNEL/SCD/SCSA (about 26% for alkaline Comet) and link values above 20-30% to worse outcomes.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Sharma R, Roychoudhury S, et al.
references.title: MiOXSYS: a novel method of measuring oxidation reduction potential in semen and seminal plasma
references.finding: Introduced MiOXSYS oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) in semen; proposed a cut-off of 1.48 mV/10^6 sperm/mL.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Panner Selvam MK, Arafa M, et al.
references.title: Multi-center evaluation of oxidation-reduction potential by the MiOXSYS in males with abnormal semen
references.finding: ORP normalised to sperm concentration flagged abnormal semen with 98.1% sensitivity but only 40.6% specificity (AUC 0.765).

references.authors: Agarwal A, Parekh N, Panner Selvam MK, et al.
references.title: Male Oxidative Stress Infertility (MOSI): Proposed Terminology and Clinical Practice Guidelines for Management of Idiopathic Male Infertility
references.finding: Proposes the term 'Male Oxidative Stress Infertility'; 30-80% of infertile men have high seminal ROS; current antioxidant use is not evidence-based.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Finelli R, Selvam MKP, et al.
references.title: A Global Survey of Reproductive Specialists to Determine the Clinical Utility of Oxidative Stress Testing and Antioxidant Use in Male Infertility
references.finding: Global survey: 85.6% of reproductive specialists prescribe antioxidants, mostly for 3-6 months, while most do not test for oxidative stress and rate the supporting evidence as modest.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Mulgund A, Alshahrani S, et al.
references.title: Reactive oxygen species and sperm DNA damage in infertile men presenting with low level leukocytospermia
references.finding: Even low-level leukocytospermia (below 1 million WBC/mL) was associated with higher ROS and SDF (26.5% vs 19.9%).

references.authors: Szabó A, Váncsa S, Hegyi P, et al.
references.title: Lifestyle-, environmental-, and additional health factors associated with an increased sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Mean SDF increase: varicocele +13.6, impaired glucose tolerance +13.8, age >=50 +12.6, air pollution +9.7, smoking +9.2 percentage points; abstinence length and chlamydia/HPV showed no clear effect.

references.authors: Sharma R, Harlev A, Agarwal A, et al.
references.title: Cigarette Smoking and Semen Quality: A New Meta-analysis Examining the Effect of the 2010 World Health Organization Laboratory Methods for the Examination of Human Semen
references.finding: Smoking lowered sperm count (-9.7 million/mL), motility (-3.5 points) and morphology; effects larger in moderate/heavy smokers and infertile men.

references.authors: Ragheb A, Abdelbary A, Massoud A, et al.
references.title: Evaluating the effect of smoking and its cessation on semen parameters
references.finding: After quitting smoking, semen improved at 3 and again at 6 months (progressive motility 20.7% -> 35.3% -> 42.3%).

references.authors: Wang YJ, Zhang RQ, Lin YJ, et al.
references.title: Relationship between varicocele and sperm DNA damage and the effect of varicocele repair: a meta-analysis
references.finding: Men with varicocele had 9.8 points more sperm DNA damage than controls; varicocelectomy lowered it by 3.4 points.

references.authors: Lira Neto FT, Roque M, Esteves SC
references.title: Effect of varicocelectomy on sperm deoxyribonucleic acid fragmentation rates in infertile men with clinical varicocele: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Varicocelectomy lowered SDF by 7.2 points (95% CI 5.6-8.9), more in men with high pre-operative SDF.

references.authors: Persad E, O'Loughlin CA, Kaur S, et al.
references.title: Surgical or radiological treatment for varicoceles in subfertile men
references.finding: Cochrane: varicocele treatment may raise pregnancy rates (RR 1.55, low certainty); effect on live birth is uncertain.

references.authors: Sepidarkish M, Maleki-Hajiagha A, Maroufizadeh S, et al.
references.title: The effect of body mass index on sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Only class I obesity (BMI 30-35) showed a small SDF increase (SMD 0.23); data insufficient for a firm BMI-SDF link.

references.authors: Campbell JM, Lane M, Owens JA, et al.
references.title: Paternal obesity negatively affects male fertility and assisted reproduction outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Obese men had more infertility (OR 1.66), lower live birth per ART cycle (OR 0.65) and more sperm DNA fragmentation.

references.authors: Sermondade N, Faure C, Fezeu L, et al.
references.title: BMI in relation to sperm count: an updated systematic review and collaborative meta-analysis
references.finding: J-shaped curve: odds of oligo/azoospermia 1.11 overweight, 1.28 obese, 2.04 morbidly obese vs normal weight.

references.authors: Santi D, Greco C, Barbonetti A, et al.
references.title: Weight Loss as Therapeutic Option to Restore Fertility in Obese Men: A Meta-Analytic Study
references.finding: Weight loss in obese men (mean baseline BMI 45) raised concentration and motility and lowered DNA fragmentation index (effect size -0.69).

references.authors: Peel A, Lyons H, Tully CA, et al.
references.title: The effect of obesity interventions on male fertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Lifestyle weight-loss programmes improved motility and morphology; bariatric surgery produced no clinically significant semen or DNA damage change; low certainty overall.

references.authors: Garolla A, Torino M, Sartini B, et al.
references.title: Seminal and molecular evidence that sauna exposure affects human spermatogenesis
references.finding: Finnish sauna (80-90 C, 15 min, twice weekly, 3 months) impaired count, motility, protamination and mitochondrial function; all effects reversed 6 months after stopping.

references.authors: Rao M, Xia W, Yang J, et al.
references.title: Transient scrotal hyperthermia affects human sperm DNA integrity, sperm apoptosis, and sperm protein expression
references.finding: Scrotal warming in a 43 C bath for 30 min x 10 sessions reversibly increased SCSA chromatin abnormality, apoptosis and mitochondrial damage; recovery by about 16 weeks.

references.authors: Shefi S, Tarapore PE, Walsh TJ, et al.
references.title: Wet heat exposure: a potentially reversible cause of low semen quality in infertile men
references.finding: After infertile men stopped hot tubs/hot baths, 5 of 11 responded with a 491% rise in total motile sperm count (motility 12% -> 34%).

references.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Gaskins AJ, Chiu YH, et al.
references.title: Type of underwear worn and markers of testicular function among men attending a fertility center
references.finding: Men who mainly wore boxers had 25% higher sperm concentration and 17% higher total count than men who did not.

references.authors: Sheynkin Y, Jung M, Yoo P, et al.
references.title: Increase in scrotal temperature in laptop computer users
references.finding: A working laptop on the lap raised scrotal temperature 2.6-2.8 C in 60 minutes (2.1 C from the closed-thigh posture alone).

references.authors: Sheynkin Y, Welliver R, Winer A, et al.
references.title: Protection from scrotal hyperthermia in laptop computer users
references.finding: Scrotal temperature rose 1 C within 11-28 minutes of laptop use; a lap pad did not prevent it; sitting with legs apart reduced it.

references.authors: Thonneau P, Bujan L, Multigner L, et al.
references.title: Occupational heat exposure and male fertility: a review
references.finding: Occupational heat exposure is a significant risk factor for male infertility, worsening morphology and delaying conception.

references.authors: Wyrobek AJ, Eskenazi B, Young S, et al.
references.title: Advancing age has differential effects on DNA damage, chromatin integrity, gene mutations, and aneuploidies in sperm
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: In healthy non-smokers, sperm DNA fragmentation index rose steadily with age, with no threshold.

references.authors: Johnson SL, Dunleavy J, Gemmell NJ, et al.
references.title: Consistent age-dependent declines in human semen quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Age was associated with declines in volume, motility, morphology and the share of unfragmented sperm.

references.authors: Ricci E, Al Beitawi S, Cipriani S, et al.
references.title: Semen quality and alcohol intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Alcohol lowered semen volume and normal morphology, mainly in daily drinkers; occasional drinking did not clearly harm semen.

references.authors: Jensen TK, Gottschau M, Madsen JO, et al.
references.title: Habitual alcohol consumption associated with reduced semen quality and changes in reproductive hormones; a cross-sectional study among 1221 young Danish men
references.finding: Habitual intake above 5 units/week was linked to poorer semen; above 40 units/week, sperm concentration was 33% lower than at 1-5 units.

references.authors: Verhaeghe F, Di Pizio P, Bichara C, et al.
references.title: Cannabis consumption might exert deleterious effects on sperm nuclear quality in infertile men
references.finding: Regular cannabis users had more sperm DNA fragmentation and aneuploidy than non-users (exploratory).

references.authors: Liu PY, Swerdloff RS, Christenson PD, et al.
references.title: Rate, extent, and modifiers of spermatogenic recovery after hormonal male contraception: an integrated analysis
references.finding: After androgen-based suppression, median time for sperm to recover to 20 million/mL was 3.4 months; longer with longer treatment.

references.authors: Rajmil O, Moreno-Sepulveda J
references.title: Recovery of spermatogenesis after androgenic anabolic steroids abuse in men. A systematic review of the literature
references.finding: Systematic review: anabolic steroid infertility is often reversible, but sperm production may take over a year to normalise.

references.authors: Rubes J, Selevan SG, Evenson DP, et al.
references.title: Episodic air pollution is associated with increased DNA fragmentation in human sperm without other changes in semen quality
references.finding: Young men in Teplice had more SCSA sperm DNA fragmentation after high-pollution periods, without other semen changes.

references.authors: Hauser R, Meeker JD, Singh NP, et al.
references.title: DNA damage in human sperm is related to urinary levels of phthalate monoester and oxidative metabolites
references.finding: Urinary phthalate metabolites MEP and MEHP were associated with more neutral-Comet sperm DNA damage (about 14-18% per IQR rise in MEHP).

references.authors: Meeker JD, Ehrlich S, Toth TL, et al.
references.title: Semen quality and sperm DNA damage in relation to urinary bisphenol A among men from an infertility clinic
references.finding: An IQR rise in urinary BPA was linked to 10% more Comet tail DNA and lower concentration and morphology.

references.authors: Miranda-Contreras L, Gómez-Pérez R, Rojas G, et al.
references.title: Occupational exposure to organophosphate and carbamate pesticides affects sperm chromatin integrity and reproductive hormone levels among Venezuelan farm workers
references.finding: Farm workers exposed to organophosphate and carbamate pesticides had higher sperm DNA fragmentation index.

references.authors: Gallegos G, Ramos B, Santiso R, et al.
references.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation in infertile men with genitourinary infection by Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma
references.finding: Chlamydia/Mycoplasma infection: SDF 35% vs 11% in fertile controls; after about 4 months of antibiotics SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2%.

references.authors: Sergerie M, Mieusset R, Croute F, et al.
references.title: High risk of temporary alteration of semen parameters after recent acute febrile illness
references.finding: After a 2-day fever of 39-40 C, DNA fragmentation index rose by 24-36% at days 15-37 and returned toward baseline by day 79.

references.authors: Coleman CM, Wesselink AK, Yland JJ, et al.
references.title: A North American preconception study of sleep health and semen quality
references.finding: Short (<6 h) or long (>=9 h) sleep and poor sleep quality were associated with roughly 15-20% lower sperm counts, with wide confidence intervals.

references.authors: Liu K, Li Y, Zhang G, et al.
references.title: Association between mobile phone use and semen quality: a systemic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: In human studies, mobile phone use had no significant effect on semen parameters; in vitro RF exposure reduced motility and viability.

references.authors: Kim S, Han D, Ryu J, et al.
references.title: Effects of mobile phone usage on sperm quality - No time-dependent relationship on usage: A systematic review and updated meta-analysis
references.finding: Phone exposure was associated with lower motility, viability and concentration, but with no dose-response by hours of use.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Desai NR, Makker K, et al.
references.title: Effects of radiofrequency electromagnetic waves (RF-EMW) from cellular phones on human ejaculated semen: an in vitro pilot study
references.finding: In vitro, phone RF exposure raised ROS and reduced motility and viability of neat semen, but did not change DNA damage.

references.authors: Gosálvez J, González-Martínez M, López-Fernández C, et al.
references.title: Shorter abstinence decreases sperm deoxyribonucleic acid fragmentation in ejaculate
references.finding: SDF was lower after 24-hour, and especially 3-hour, abstinence than after the standard abstinence period.

references.authors: Barbagallo F, Cannarella R, Crafa A, et al.
references.title: The Impact of a Very Short Abstinence Period on Conventional Sperm Parameters and Sperm DNA Fragmentation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: A second ejaculate within 4 hours had lower SDF in men with abnormal semen.

references.authors: Lo Giudice A, Asmundo MG, Cimino S, et al.
references.title: Effects of long and short ejaculatory abstinence on sperm parameters: a meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials
references.finding: Abstinence longer than 2 days was associated with SDF 3.5 points higher; each extra day added about 0.65 points.

references.authors: Du C, Li Y, Yin C, et al.
references.title: Association of abstinence time with semen quality and fertility outcomes: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
references.finding: Short versus long abstinence lowered DNA fragmentation index by about 2.4 points in healthy men, at the cost of lower volume and count.

references.authors: Dahan MH, Mills G, Khoudja R, et al.
references.title: Three hour abstinence as a treatment for high sperm DNA fragmentation: a prospective cohort study
references.finding: SDF fell from 34.6% after 3 days of abstinence to 23.7% in a second sample 3 hours later; 55% of men with SDF >35% moved into the normal range.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Mendiola J, Afeiche M, et al.
references.title: Physical activity and television watching in relation to semen quality in young men
references.finding: Men with >=15 h/week moderate-vigorous activity had 73% higher sperm concentration; >20 h/week TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

references.authors: Wise LA, Cramer DW, Hornstein MD, et al.
references.title: Physical activity and semen quality among men attending an infertility clinic
references.finding: Regular exercise overall was unrelated to semen quality, but cycling >=5 h/week was linked to low concentration (OR 1.92) and low total motile count.

references.authors: Hajizadeh Maleki B, Tartibian B, Chehrazi M
references.title: The effects of three different exercise modalities on markers of male reproduction in healthy subjects: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: 24 weeks of moderate continuous training improved seminal oxidative and inflammatory markers and sperm DNA integrity more than high-intensity training (same group has several retracted trials).

references.authors: Hajizadeh Maleki B, Tartibian B
references.title: Long-term Low-to-Intensive Cycling Training: Impact on Semen Parameters and Seminal Cytokines
references.finding: 16 weeks of intensive road-cycling training raised seminal cytokines and worsened semen; some changes persisted 30 days after training.

references.authors: Robbins WA, Xun L, FitzGerald LZ, et al.
references.title: Walnuts improve semen quality in men consuming a Western-style diet: randomized control dietary intervention trial
references.finding: Adding 75 g/day walnuts for 12 weeks improved sperm vitality, motility and morphology (DNA fragmentation not measured).

references.authors: Salas-Huetos A, Moraleda R, Giardina S, et al.
references.title: Effect of nut consumption on semen quality and functionality in healthy men consuming a Western-style diet: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Adding 60 g/day mixed nuts for 14 weeks improved count, vitality, motility and morphology and reduced sperm DNA fragmentation.

references.authors: Karayiannis D, Kontogianni MD, Mendorou C, et al.
references.title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and semen quality parameters in male partners of couples attempting fertility
references.finding: Men in the lowest Mediterranean-diet tertile had about 2.6 times the odds of abnormal concentration, count and motility.

references.authors: Agarwal R, Salas-Salvadó J, Davila-Cordova E, et al.
references.title: Mediterranean Diet, Semen Quality, and Medically Assisted Reproductive Outcomes in the Male Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Mediterranean diet adherence was associated with higher sperm count (+24 million), motility (+8.8 points) and morphology; no data showing better fertility outcomes.

references.authors: Salas-Huetos A, Bulló M, Salas-Salvadó J
references.title: Dietary patterns, foods and nutrients in male fertility parameters and fecundability: a systematic review of observational studies
references.finding: Systematic review of observational studies: diets rich in fish, fruit, vegetables and whole grains go with better semen; processed meat, sugary drinks, alcohol and soy with worse semen in some studies.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Colaci DS, Mendiola J, et al.
references.title: Dietary patterns and semen quality in young men
references.finding: Young men in the top quartile of a 'prudent' diet (fish, chicken, fruit, vegetables, legumes, whole grains) had 11.3 points higher progressive motility.

references.authors: Afeiche MC, Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Processed meat intake is unfavorably and fish intake favorably associated with semen quality indicators among men attending a fertility clinic
references.finding: Highest processed-meat quartile had 1.7 points fewer normal forms; total count rose from 102 to 168 million across fish-intake quartiles.

references.authors: Chiu YH, Afeiche MC, Gaskins AJ, et al.
references.title: Sugar-sweetened beverage intake in relation to semen quality and reproductive hormone levels in young men
references.finding: Young men drinking >=1.3 sugar-sweetened beverages/day had 9.8 points lower progressive motility than those drinking <0.2/day.

references.authors: Chiu YH, Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Intake of Fruits and Vegetables with Low-to-Moderate Pesticide Residues Is Positively Associated with Semen-Quality Parameters among Young Healthy Men
references.finding: Eating >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-pesticide fruit and vegetables was linked to 169% higher total sperm count; high-pesticide produce was not.

references.authors: Williams EA, Parker M, Robinson A, et al.
references.title: A randomized placebo-controlled trial to investigate the effect of lactolycopene on semen quality in healthy males
references.finding: 14 mg/day lactolycopene for 12 weeks improved fast progressive motility and morphology; the primary endpoint was not significant.

references.authors: Ricci E, Viganò P, Cipriani S, et al.
references.title: Coffee and caffeine intake and male infertility: a systematic review
references.finding: Caffeine from coffee and tea was mostly unrelated to semen parameters; caffeinated soft drinks looked harmful; DNA-damage findings inconsistent.

references.authors: Chavarro JE, Toth TL, Sadio SM, et al.
references.title: Soy food and isoflavone intake in relation to semen quality parameters among men from an infertility clinic
references.finding: Men in the highest soy-food category had 41 million/mL lower sperm concentration; no link to motility or morphology.

references.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Afeiche MC, Chiu YH, et al.
references.title: Male soy food intake was not associated with in vitro fertilization outcomes among couples attending a fertility center
references.finding: Male partners' soy intake was unrelated to fertilization, embryo quality or live birth in IVF.

references.authors: Reed KE, Camargo J, Hamilton-Reeves J, et al.
references.title: Neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones: An expanded and updated meta-analysis of clinical studies
references.finding: Soy protein and isoflavones did not change testosterone, free testosterone, estrogens or SHBG in men.

references.authors: Falsig AL, Gleerup CS, Knudsen UB
references.title: The influence of omega-3 fatty acids on semen quality markers: a systematic PRISMA review
references.finding: 14 of 16 studies found omega-3 intake or supplements associated with improvement in at least one semen marker; studies too heterogeneous to pool.

references.authors: Jensen TK, Priskorn L, Holmboe SA, et al.
references.title: Associations of Fish Oil Supplement Use With Testicular Function in Young Men
references.finding: Young men using fish oil supplements on >=60 days had 0.64 mL more semen volume, larger testes and lower FSH and LH.

references.authors: Martínez-Soto JC, Domingo JC, Cordobilla B, et al.
references.title: Dietary supplementation with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) improves seminal antioxidant status and decreases sperm DNA fragmentation
references.finding: 1.5 g/day DHA for 10 weeks improved seminal antioxidant status and lowered sperm DNA fragmentation, without changing standard parameters.

references.authors: Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Yazdani A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
references.finding: Cochrane 2019: live birth OR 1.79 (7 RCTs, 750 men, low-quality evidence); no significant benefit once high-risk-of-bias trials were removed (Peto OR 1.38, 0.89-2.16).

references.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
references.finding: Cochrane 2022: live birth OR 1.43 (very low certainty); after removing high-risk-of-bias trials, no significant benefit (OR 1.22, 0.85-1.75).

references.authors: Steiner AZ, Hansen KR, Barnhart KT, et al.
references.title: The effect of antioxidants on male factor infertility: the Males, Antioxidants, and Infertility (MOXI) randomized clinical trial
references.finding: MOXI: a 7-ingredient antioxidant for 3-6 months did not improve semen parameters or DNA fragmentation; live birth 15% vs 24% placebo.

references.authors: Schisterman EF, Sjaarda LA, Clemons T, et al.
references.title: Effect of Folic Acid and Zinc Supplementation in Men on Semen Quality and Live Birth Among Couples Undergoing Infertility Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: FAZST: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc for 6 months did not improve semen or live birth (34% vs 35%); DNA fragmentation slightly higher (29.7% vs 27.2%).

references.authors: Greco E, Romano S, Iacobelli M, et al.
references.title: ICSI in cases of sperm DNA damage: beneficial effect of oral antioxidant treatment
references.finding: 1 g vitamin C + 1 g vitamin E daily for 2 months lowered SDF in 76% of men; the next ICSI had 48.2% vs 6.9% pregnancy (uncontrolled before-after).

references.authors: Ménézo YJ, Hazout A, Panteix G, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants to reduce sperm DNA fragmentation: an unexpected adverse effect
references.finding: 90 days of antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium lowered DFI by 19% but raised sperm decondensation by 23%.

references.authors: Moazamian A, Hug E, Villeneuve P, et al.
references.title: The dual nature of micronutrients on fertility: too much of a good thing?
references.finding: In healthy mice, high doses of vitamin C, zinc, folate or carnitine disturbed redox balance and damaged sperm DNA; high carnitine cut pregnancy rates, but helped oxidatively stressed mice.

references.authors: Stenqvist A, Oleszczuk K, Leijonhufvud I, et al.
references.title: Impact of antioxidant treatment on DNA fragmentation index: a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trial
references.finding: Six months of combined antioxidants did not lower DNA fragmentation index in men with DFI >=25%.

references.authors: Tremellen K, Miari G, Froiland D, et al.
references.title: A randomised control trial examining the effect of an antioxidant (Menevit) on pregnancy outcome during IVF-ICSI treatment
references.journal: Aust N Z J Obstet Gynaecol
references.finding: Menevit for 3 months before IVF-ICSI: viable pregnancy 38.5% vs 16% per transferred embryo; embryo quality unchanged.

references.authors: Kopets R, Kuibida I, Chernyavska I, et al.
references.title: Dietary supplementation with a novel l-carnitine multi-micronutrient in idiopathic male subfertility involving oligo-, astheno-, teratozoospermia: A randomized clinical study
references.finding: An L-carnitine multi-micronutrient for 6 months raised the share of normal semen analyses (69% vs 22%) and spontaneous pregnancies.

references.authors: Lafuente R, González-Comadrán M, Solà I, et al.
references.title: Coenzyme Q10 and male infertility: a meta-analysis
references.finding: CoQ10 raised sperm concentration and motility, but there was no evidence for higher pregnancy or live birth.

references.authors: Balercia G, Buldreghini E, Vignini A, et al.
references.title: Coenzyme Q10 treatment in infertile men with idiopathic asthenozoospermia: a placebo-controlled, double-blind randomized trial
references.finding: CoQ10 200 mg/day for 6 months increased seminal CoQ10 and motility in idiopathic asthenozoospermia.

references.authors: Comhaire FH, El Garem Y, Mahmoud A, et al.
references.title: Combined conventional/antioxidant "Astaxanthin" treatment for male infertility: a double blind, randomized trial
references.finding: Astaxanthin 16 mg/day for 3 months lowered seminal ROS; pregnancy 54.5% vs 10.5% in a very small trial.

references.authors: Khaw SC, Wong ZZ, Anderson R, et al.
references.title: l-carnitine and l-acetylcarnitine supplementation for idiopathic male infertility
references.finding: Carnitines improved total and progressive motility and morphology, with no demonstrable effect on clinical pregnancy.

references.authors: Salas-Huetos A, Rosique-Esteban N, Becerra-Tomás N, et al.
references.title: The Effect of Nutrients and Dietary Supplements on Sperm Quality Parameters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
references.finding: Selenium, zinc, omega-3, CoQ10 and carnitines produced modest improvements in sperm parameters; fertility outcomes not assessed.

references.authors: Jannatifar R, Parivar K, Roodbari NH, et al.
references.title: Effects of N-acetyl-cysteine supplementation on sperm quality, chromatin integrity and level of oxidative stress in infertile men
references.finding: NAC 600 mg/day for 3 months lowered SDF and protamine deficiency and improved count and motility (uncontrolled before-after).

references.authors: Scott R, MacPherson A, Yates RW, et al.
references.title: The effect of oral selenium supplementation on human sperm motility
references.finding: Selenium (with or without vitamins A, C, E) for 3 months raised motility in subfertile Scottish men with low selenium; 11% paternity vs 0%.

references.authors: Blomberg Jensen M, Lawaetz JG, Petersen JH, et al.
references.title: Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation on Semen Quality, Reproductive Hormones, and Live Birth Rate: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: Vitamin D (300,000 IU then 1400 IU/day) plus calcium for 150 days did not improve semen quality in vitamin-D-insufficient infertile men.
